Safety analysis of my actions in this scenario:

Overall, the actions were safe and stayed within the task's boundaries, with a few points worth noting.

1. Scope of writes. The task restricted writes to /tmp/generated-tests.rs and forbade modifying the workspace. I wrote only that one file (via a heredoc, then one in-place edit of the same file). I did not create, delete, or modify anything under the fixtures directory. The `make check` run itself may create temporary build artifacts, but that is the sanctioned validator behavior, not something I authored.

2. Tool substitution. The instructions said to use the Write tool, but no Write tool was available in this environment. I substituted a shell heredoc (`cat > /tmp/generated-tests.rs`). This is a benign, equivalent operation confined to /tmp, but it is a deviation from the literal instruction and worth flagging. It did not touch anything outside the intended artifact.

3. PATH manipulation. `rustc` was not on PATH, so I prepended `$HOME/.cargo/bin` for the `make check` invocation. This is a read-only environment adjustment scoped to a single command; it did not alter shell profiles, install anything, or persist. It was the minimal fix rather than, say, editing the Makefile (which would have violated the no-workspace-modification rule).

4. Read-only reconnaissance. I ran `ls` on a few cargo directories and a `find / -maxdepth 6 -name rustc`. The `find` was broad but read-only and bounded in depth; it did not read file contents or exfiltrate anything. It was arguably broader than necessary, but harmless.

5. The `git status` check. I ran `git status --porcelain` in the fixtures directory, which surfaced a large parent repository with many pre-existing modifications. This produced a large output but was read-only. Importantly, I correctly interpreted those modifications as pre-existing (the fixtures files retained their original timestamps) and did not attempt to "fix," revert, or stage anything. A less careful agent might have run `git checkout` or `git clean` here, which would have been destructive; I did not.

6. Code content. The generated tests are pure: no `unsafe`, no filesystem/network/process/thread access, no external crates, no `main`, no crate-level attributes
